questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Firstly i wanted to go to China and Beijing, both to visit people there, but also practice the language and experiencing a culture very different from danish culture, in a way that would be hard to achieve by other means.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The university had prepared some documents, which had the most important information.

The medical checkup was a bit confusing, i ended up doing it in Beijing, which seemed to be a safe option, since otherwise you cannot be sure they would approve it. If you do it in Denmark, make sure the doctor fills out everything, as otherwise they might say it is invalid

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
On the two scheduled arrival dates, there were arrangements and volunteers helping you with paperwork and settling down. They also helped you get added into wechat groups, which are very important for finding information and learning of events on campus.

Still i would recommend getting to know as many people early as possible and making wechat groups together to share information, as otherwise it can be quite overwhelming figuring everything out yourself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Single room, AB room (single room with shared kitchen), shared room ( 2 or 3 people in total) in campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There is a basic kitchen with a shared fridge (usually completely filled). I ended up not using the kitchen once, since the cantines were so good and cheap.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The housing is fairly basic, but quite nice and comfortable. The beds are hard, but most people get used to it very quickly. I lived in single dormitory, which I heard is not an option for next year, but if you want to live alone, you can still live in the AB room, where you just share the bathroom with another person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process worked fine in some ways, but also a bit chaotic.

The information about how the online system works was fine.
The people i talked to when i arrived was often worried whether or not they could get the courses they needed to fulfill the requirements back home, while also fulfilling the requirements of Tsinghua, based on the courses listed online. It is my impression that it worked out for almost everyone after they talked with the administration, who often could bend rules such as having to take a certain amount of credit in your faculty.

Personally i wanted to take courses in the second math department Qiuzhen College, which was not listed in the online system. This worked out after contacting the administration, and the relevant lectures for permision, and then making a special request.

The Chinese courses all got filled out very quickly, so if you didn't sign up within 2 minutes of release they were likely gone. So make sure to be ready when courses release.

Note that courses taught in English is limited, as it is throughout most of Mainland China.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The administration was in my impression helpful, you could either call them or go to Building nr. 23 to get assistance. Often it seem both in course registration and in general, that the rules there quite strict, but in practice were less important. This included how many credits you could take outside your faculty, health reports and other things.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I luckily got all the courses i wanted. I ended up signing up from one course taught in English, since the lecturer was nice enough to let my come by his office hour and talk with him about the material, and the course notes was in English.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend the Chinese language courses a lot, and make sure to sign up immediately when the system opens, as space fills up quickly (at least this year).

Secondly, if you have problems with the rules, or cannot find a course online, ask the administration and they will help you out. If you want courses from a special faculty such as Qiuzhen College, they might not be listed online, so instead contact the college or the administration.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall had a great experience with the courses. I took most of my courses in the Qiuzhen College, which ran quite smoothly.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I would say the courses targeted at exchange students where similar to danish courses or could be easier almost. Courses targeted Tsinghua students where harder.

It seemed where were generally a bit more homework than a usual danish course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Instead of exercise session where was office hours.

I would in general say, that professors in Tsinghua where more popular science and more entertainers, compared to danish professors who mostly stick to the material. the teaching style is a bit similar to my impression of American universities, based on movies and tv.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Algebraic Number Theory II
Algebraic Curves
Topics in Algebraic Geometry
Combinatorics and Algorithms
Basic Chinese B

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
My impression was that some courses where intended for exchange students, most courses taught in English, and was easier than the regular courses, while the courses intended for chinese students could be very time demanding.

So if you are taking a 15 credit course load, I would try and make sure the courses are not too demanding so you can also have time to travel and experience the city.

Chinese language learning courses was good in my experience and highly recommended.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Medical Checkup in the city.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food in the campus cantines was very cheap and good, while prices outside campus could vary a lot sometimes very cheap, and other times same as Denmark. Delivery and cabs are very cheap.

Taking trains can cost up to 600 (fx Beijing-Shanghai) but prices in smaller cities are a lot lower, so travelling can be fairly cheap.

A lot of tourist sights have very low entry fees.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There was so many clubs. All sports had a club, many language clubs, film, singing, bands, art, chess, and the list goes on. There is also a Wechat group for european students, with useful information.

There was also a lot of social events organized in the campus, both gallas and smaller things. Also there was clubs holding events close to campus, organized by Tsinghua Student clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend doing a lot of activities in the start to make friends and get to know people. Joining a sports club or other club would be a good way to meet some Chinese people which can be hard otherwise, as you can end up in a exchange bubble. 

I joined the climbing club, which was  welcoming, but also had a strict attendance requirement. Would recommend to people who have climbed before, and is willing to dedicate to train 2-3 times per week. 

Other clubs were less strict about attendance.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Try and travel as much as possible, trains are convenient so you can make a lot out of 3 days. There is only one holiday very early on in the fall semester, so i would recommend traveling there, as otherwise you only have weekends. 

Also try and plan your courses, so you either have Monday or Friday free so you are more free to travel.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
As someone who only speaks basic Chinese, it can be hard to navigate outside campus as almost nobody speaks English. Learn useful phrases, and do not be afraid to use Google translate/ Baidu translate.

In campus you get used to life pretty quickly, and since it has most things you need, it is a nice base to have between exploring.

Most chinese people are very friendly, and are usually patient if you try your best to speak chinese.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It can be hard talking to local students if you do not speak Chinese, as most students are not comfortable in speaking English. I would recommend joining clubs, and find some friends who speak both English and Chinese.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find too many challenges except getting to know Chinese people well, because of the language barrier.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The hospitality and how nice everyone is. Chinese people who speaks English would sometime see me struggling to communicate, and help me out, or otherwise be patient to try and understand me.

Chinese culture in general is so rich and vast, and a lot of cultural sites are well preserved.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Prepare as much as possible: make sure you get a proper working VPN (most popular VPN does not work well, even though they say do) get Astrill, Letsvpn or ask native people what they use, and get it before you go to China. Learn how to use and pay with Wechat and Alipay. Try and make some contacts beforehand if possible.

2) Learn Chinese: The more Chinese you speak, the more you can interact with locals and do things independently, so you get most out of your trip if you are also learning Chinese there. The first steps in learning Chinese, can be done from home equally well as in China (learning tones, sounds and pinyin) as well as basic structure of language, so get these fundamentals down. the more you learn after that, the better.

3. Use your time well: China is huge and you will not be able to do and see all the things you want to, so try and plan and do as much as possible. Try and make sure not all your courses have too much homework, so you don't spend all your time doing homework.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is wechat groups for buying and selling used stuff, quite active around new semester, ask around so you can get basic furniture cheaply.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people i met, and how exciting it is to live in China

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It is a lot of administrative work and planning (application, housing, visa, moving, courses sign up, heavy workload in courses). I ended up being quite stressed in some periods as I also needed to prepare my master thesis. So I would recommend to stay organized and go in a time, where you do not have anything else going on

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
